A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
inventory
A description or list of items being kept.
underlying
Existing beneath a summary or description.
headcount
The total number of people in a group.
misconduct
Unacceptable or improper behaviour.
challenge a decision
To ask for a decision to be reconsidered.
transparency
Openness about how decisions are made.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

0:00 / 0:00

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Three headings filled the page in front of Emma: Applied, Selected, Paid. They had given her a way to organise the uncertainty, but not yet a reliable figure for any of the stages. Fiona Bell had located a partial list of application references; the trust was still considering what could be disclosed without identifying former students.

The following morning Fiona rang. The records team had completed a preliminary description of the surviving papers. The visible references began at eleven and ran as far as twenty-six, with several gaps. The figures sounded promising until Emma asked whether the final reference indicated the total number of applications.

“Not necessarily,” Fiona said. “A reference could have been reserved for a form that was never submitted. And we haven't established whether the numbering began again at any point.”

Fiona could provide an inventory description, but not the underlying list or names. She had also seen the decision section on the blank form; she had not located a complete membership record for the selection panel.

Emma kept the distinction clear in her notes: a description of records, reported by Fiona, was not the same as examining those records herself.

Sarah was enthusiastic when they spoke at lunchtime. “At least we can say there were twenty-six applicants.”

“We can't. Twenty-six is the highest reference Fiona mentioned, not a confirmed headcount.”

Emma searched the newspaper archive again and located a small report from early October 2011. It said that several students were still waiting for news about travel support. It offered no names, and it failed to distinguish between applicants waiting for a decision and successful candidates waiting for payment.

“That may explain why families were frustrated,” Sarah said.

“Perhaps. But we can't work backwards from a report of delays to a claim of misconduct.”

They saved the item and its publication date, retaining the original wording rather than rewriting it as a stronger allegation. Emma drafted a separate request about the selection process, asking whether a policy had provided for unsuccessful applicants to challenge decisions. She did not send it immediately. Fiona was already trying to identify what records existed, and Emma wanted to avoid confusing a document request with an accusation.

That evening an email arrived from Fiona. A folder in storage had a covering sheet headed “Appeals and reviews — Student Travel 2011”. Fiona stressed that she had not inspected its contents. The title could refer to actual challenges, standard paperwork or a procedure never used.

Emma read the note twice. The parent's letter from September had complained about a lack of transparency. Now she had a heading that might lead towards the way decisions were reconsidered.

She wrote a new question: Was an appeal possible—and did anyone make one?

This time she had a precise next step, not a suspect.
